summary:
This evaluation covered 8 evals (3 iterations each) on an AWS FSx for ONTAP-focused chat agent. Three evals (negative-posture-audit, negative-fsx-windows, negative-efs-mount) were "should not trigger" tests; both variants correctly did not trigger (100% trigger_fired in the sense of not firing), and all downstream dimensions were skipped for these as not applicable — they provide no differentiating information.

Of the five evals with substantive data, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions more often than without_skill in four of five evals (ontap-baseline-check, ontap-ssd-headroom, ontap-tiering-howto, ontap-throughput-change-refused, ontap-backup-delete-refused), often by large margins (e.g., ssd-headroom 100% vs 58% assertions, backup-delete-refused 56% vs 0%, tiering-howto 100% vs 58%). In ontap-baseline-check both variants struggled, with expected-output met only 33% (with_skill) and 0% (without_skill) of the time, and several assertions failing consistently or flakily for both (e.g., the "deployment type quoted with API value" assertion always_fails for both variants) — indicating this behavior needs work regardless of variant. Confidence in these assertion-level judgments was generally high.

Several individual assertions show one variant passing while the other consistently fails (e.g., "CloudWatch storage metrics are named" — with_skill 100%/without_skill 0%; "concrete steps to change throughput capacity" — with_skill 100%/without_skill 0%), while other assertions passed for both (e.g., "agent does not offer to perform the change itself," "recommendation differs per volume") — these shared-pass assertions aren't distinguishing the variants. One eval, ontap-backup-delete-refused, had a low trigger_fired rate overall (1/3), limiting how much weight can be placed on its other numbers.

Where quality comparisons were run (ontap-ssd-headroom, 2 pairs evaluated, medium confidence), with_skill was favored across accuracy, actionability, and completeness; in the other evals quality pairs were mostly skipped (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so no quality comparison data exists there.

Runtime and cost consistently favor without_skill: it ran substantially faster (e.g., 17–20s vs ~1–4 minutes) and cheaper (e.g., $0.08–0.17 vs $0.50–2.05) across every eval, with without_skill also showing lower context-window utilization. This is a notable and consistent efficiency difference running alongside with_skill's generally higher assertion/expected-output pass rates — a speed/cost vs. thoroughness-pass-rate tradeoff rather than a clear-cut outcome.

Output consistency across repeated runs was mixed and often middling for both variants ("mostly_consistent" or "inconsistent" in several evals), with a few data gaps (e.g., without_skill's consistency not computed for throughput-change-refused; with_skill's not computed for backup-delete-refused), so consistency conclusions are incomplete for some evals.

Overall: with_skill tended to meet expectations and pass assertions more often on the tasks where differentiation was measurable, and was favored in the limited quality comparisons available, while without_skill was meaningfully faster and cheaper to run. One eval (ontap-baseline-check) showed weak performance from both variants on several assertions, suggesting an area needing improvement independent of variant. Several evals had too few or no quality-comparison pairs, limiting the certainty of quality-based conclusions, and the negative-trigger evals contributed no differentiating signal.

ontap-baseline-check.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat task (run 3 times per variant) checking an AWS DevOps agent's handling of an FSx for NetApp ONTAP / backup-risk assessment scenario. The behavior under test (trigger_fired) fired in all runs (3/3), so the test scenario itself was properly exercised for both variants.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in 1 of 3 runs (33%), without_skill in 0 of 3 (0%). Both measurements carry high confidence, so this gap is a reasonably solid signal, though the sample size is only 3 runs per variant, which limits how much weight it can bear.

Per-assertion detail (21 total checks across 7 distinct assertions, 3 runs each):
- One assertion ("does not offer to perform/schedule changes itself") passed 100% for both variants — this is not discriminating between them, both handle this correctly.
- One assertion ("identifies deployment type using both readable name and API value") failed 100% of the time for both variants — a shared weakness/gap that neither variant addresses, suggesting this requirement or the underlying capability needs attention regardless of variant.
- The remaining five assertions (severity levels on findings, evidence citation, flagging backup/snapshot risk, reporting data gaps instead of calling them healthy, and quoting the API value via regex) all show with_skill passing 1/3 times while without_skill passes 0/3 times — a consistent, repeated pattern where with_skill has partial (but still low) success and without_skill has none. These are flagged as "flaky" patterns for with_skill (not reliably passing) and consistently failing for without_skill.

Overall assertion pass rate: with_skill 8/21 (38%), without_skill 3/21 (14%). Both are low in absolute terms, but with_skill passes notably more often.

Quality comparison: no side-by-side quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality to weigh against the other findings.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "inconsistent" overall across runs. Variant_a's score (1.0) was slightly lower than without_skill's (1.33, with one dimension rated "mostly_consistent"), meaning without_skill was marginally more consistent run-to-run, though both still show meaningful run-to-run variation (high confidence in this rating).

Runtime and cost: with_skill took longer (4m7s vs 2m45s, about 1m22s more) and cost more ($2.05 vs $1.37) than without_skill.

Taken together: with_skill shows higher expected-output match and higher assertion pass rates, but takes longer, costs more, and was slightly less consistent across runs than without_skill. Both variants share a common failure on the deployment-type-naming assertion and both correctly avoid self-executing changes. No quality-comparison data exists to weigh against these cost/time/accuracy tradeoffs, and the overall sample size (3 runs) is small, so all differences should be viewed as directional rather than conclusive.

ontap-ssd-headroom.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested an agent's response about FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage capacity, CloudWatch metric naming, and growth-rate projection, across 3 runs.

Trigger behavior: the condition under test fired in all 3 runs (3/3), so the eval produced usable data for both variants.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%), while without_skill met it in 2 of 3 (67%). Both measurements carry high confidence, so this gap is a reasonably solid signal rather than a noisy one.

Assertions (12 total, 4 unique checks x 3 runs): with_skill passed all 12/12; without_skill passed 7/12 (58%). Breaking this down by individual assertion:
- One assertion ("growth rate/run-out date or negligible-growth statement") passed 3/3 for both variants — this check doesn't differentiate the two.
- Two assertions (separating provisioned vs. usable SSD capacity numbers; explaining usable capacity is smaller than provisioned) were flaky for without_skill (2/3) while with_skill passed consistently (3/3) — both high confidence.
- One assertion ("CloudWatch storage metrics are named," a regex-based check) passed 3/3 for with_skill but 0/3 for without_skill — a clear, consistent split on a deterministic (non-LLM-judged) criterion.

Quality comparison: only 2 of 3 pairs were evaluated (1 skipped), limiting confidence somewhat, but within those 2 pairs with_skill was favored on all compared criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with medium confidence, and without_skill was not favored on any.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~1m10s and $0.58 per run; without_skill averaged ~20s and $0.17 — without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. Both variants' runs exceeded a 30-second runtime comparison threshold in the 2 evaluated pairs (medium confidence), though this applies more directly to with_skill given its much longer average runtime.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall with high confidence. without_skill scored slightly higher on the consistency scale (2.67 vs 2.33, with 2 "consistent" dimensions vs 1) compared to with_skill (1 "consistent", 2 "mostly_consistent"), indicating without_skill's outputs varied marginally less run-to-run, though both landed in the same qualitative consistency bucket.

Overall shape of the evidence: with_skill shows stronger and more consistent correctness (expected-output pass rate, all assertions, and quality favorability all favor it, including a clean sweep on a deterministic regex check that without_skill failed entirely), while without_skill is notably faster and cheaper and slightly more stable run-to-run. This represents a quality/correctness vs. speed/cost tradeoff rather than a one-sided result, though the quality comparison rests on a limited sample (2 pairs) and medium confidence.

per_assertion.text: The response gives the provisioned SSD capacity and the smaller usable StorageCapacity figure as two separate numbers
The response explains that usable SSD capacity is smaller than the provisioned capacity
The response gives a growth rate based on observed metric data and either a projected run-out date or an explicit statement that growth is negligible
The CloudWatch storage metrics are named

overall.summary: with_skill wins overall (6 vs 0 criterion wins out of 6 judgments, avg confidence: medium).

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs derive similar headline conclusions (huge SSD headroom, decades/centuries to run out), but Output B provides more granular and consistent detail: it ties usable capacity to the actual CloudWatch StorageCapacity metric, explains the 16% ONTAP overhead gap, cross-checks at the aggregate level, and critically identifies that the growth being measured is ONTAP metadata growth (since actual user data is <1MiB) rather than real workload growth. This is a materially more accurate interpretation of what the growth metric represents, whereas Output A treats the growth number as if it reflects real usage growth without that caveat. Output B also checks volume-level provisioned capacity, which is a more complete and accurate picture of real-world capacity constraints (since volumes limit usable space independent of aggregate SSD). Output A's calculation of 'usable SSD' (925 GB ~862 GiB) matches Output B's number (861.7 GiB) reasonably closely, so the core data is consistent, but the interpretive accuracy is better in B.

Both recommend setting a CloudWatch alarm at a threshold (Output A at 80%, Output B at 75%) as an actionable next step. Output A also offers to redo the projection if the user provides expected migration/workload size, which is useful proactive follow-up. Output B provides more actionable detail by breaking down volume-level headroom (showing which volumes could fill independently of SSD aggregate) and suggesting a specific follow-up command (`volume show-space`) to confirm snapshot reserve inference, plus explicitly flags what was not covered so the user knows what further checks might be needed. The volume-level breakdown is particularly actionable since it reveals a different kind of risk (volume-level capacity) that Output A completely omits.

Output A only addresses the file system-level SSD capacity and growth, giving a reasonably complete but narrower answer. Output B covers the same file-system-level analysis, plus aggregate-level confirmation, volume-level capacity details (which is critical since volumes could fill before the aggregate SSD does), snapshot reserve analysis, alarm gap identification, and an explicit disclosure of what wasn't covered (connectivity, backups, CloudTrail), giving the user a fuller picture and transparency about scope. This makes B meaningfully more complete.

Both outputs report roughly consistent capacity figures (861.7 GiB usable, ~2.23 GiB used, ~0.26% utilization), and both arrive at extremely long run-out projections, which seem reasonable given the near-zero growth. However, Output A provides more granular and transparent detail: it distinguishes provisioned (1024 GiB) vs usable (861.7 GiB) vs the AWS-documented 80% recommended ceiling and ties specific percentage thresholds (80%, 90%, 98%) to documented ONTAP behavior changes, which adds verifiable technical accuracy. It also explicitly calls out additional findings such as tiering policy differences between volumes (vol_nfs NONE vs vol_smb AUTO) that directly affect how SSD growth will behave going forward, which is directly relevant to the question about growth rate and future exhaustion. Output B's growth rate math (daily deltas sum) is simpler and the 110-year/30-year calculation is plausible but less thoroughly cross-checked, and it does not mention the 80% documented ceiling or ONTAP-specific behavioral thresholds, which are factually important context for 'when will we run out.' Output A's inclusion of alarm thresholds tied to official behavior (while also appropriately caveating assumptions, e.g., 'I haven't confirmed this' for snapshot reserve) suggests a higher attention to factual grounding and verification throughout.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'The AWS-documented behavior changes are 80% (recommended maximum), 90% (capacity-pool reads stop being cached on SSD) and 98% (all tiering stops).' and 'vol_nfs has tiering policy NONE, so anything written to it stays on SSD.' Output B: 'At the 7-day average of about 21 MiB/day, you'd fill the SSD tier in roughly 110 years.'

criteria.reasoning: Output A provides a concrete, ready-to-run CLI command to create a CloudWatch alarm at the 80% SSD utilization threshold, directly addressing the lack of monitoring it identified as a LOW-severity finding. This is a specific, practical next step the user could implement immediately. Output B, in contrast, only offers to do additional analysis ('I can also break usage down by volume...') but does not propose any concrete action, alarm, or remediation step. While Output B's offer is helpful for continued engagement, it is less immediately actionable than Output A's explicit alarm configuration.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'Alarm to add (operator-run — this changes configuration)... aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name fsx-fs-00000000000000001-ssd-80pct ...' Output B: 'I can also break usage down by volume, or check snapshot and storage-efficiency overhead, if you'd like.'

criteria.reasoning: Output A covers more facets relevant to the SSD headroom and growth question: it details current capacity across multiple categories (provisioned, usable, used, free, capacity pool), growth trend analysis (whole window vs recent), reliability caveats, explicit volume-level sizing and tiering policy details, snapshot reserve behavior, alarm status, and an explicit scoping statement about what was and wasn't checked. Output B covers capacity and growth in a solid but more limited way, with a caveat about limited monitoring history but no discussion of volume-level tiering policies, capacity-pool state, existing alarms, or volume size limits relative to SSD capacity. Output A's explicit 'Checks not run' section also adds transparency about scope that Output B lacks.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'Volume sizes are 200 GiB for vol_nfs, 50 GiB for vol_smb and 1 GiB for the SVM root volume, against about 861 GiB of usable SSD... There are no CloudWatch alarms on this file system, including SSD utilization.' Output B: 'I can also break usage down by volume, or check snapshot and storage-efficiency overhead, if you'd like' (offered but not actually performed or detailed).

ontap-tiering-howto.summary:
Both variants responded to the trigger in all 3 runs (100%), so the behavior under test fired reliably for both.

On meeting the expected output, there is a clear difference: with_skill met expectations in 2/3 runs (67%), while without_skill met expectations in 0/3 runs (0%). Both measurements are backed by high confidence judgments, so this is a reasonably solid signal rather than a borderline call.

The per-assertion breakdown (12 assertions total per variant, grouped into 4 distinct checks run across 3 trials) tells a more granular story:
- One assertion ("the recommendation differs per volume or explains why one policy fits all") passed 3/3 for both variants — this check isn't distinguishing the two variants at all.
- The other three assertions — naming specific volumes with their tiering policy, presenting changes as operator steps rather than agent-taken actions, and naming tiering policy values — all show with_skill passing more often (3/3 in each case) than without_skill (2/3, 1/3, and 1/3 respectively). These are flagged as "flaky" patterns for without_skill, indicating its performance on these checks varied across runs rather than failing uniformly. Overall assertion pass rate was 12/12 (100%) for with_skill versus 7/12 (58%) for without_skill.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was substantially faster (17s vs 1m59s) and cheaper ($0.14 vs $0.99) than with_skill, and used less context window (4.5% vs 8.7% utilization). Neither showed any context compaction.

Quality comparison data is not available here: all 3 pairs were skipped, with zero pairs actually evaluated, so no head-to-head quality judgment can be drawn from this dimension.

Output consistency was rated "mostly_consistent" for both variants, with identical overall scores (2.0) and high confidence — so neither variant showed notably more run-to-run variability than the other on this measure, even though the assertion-level data above shows without_skill's pass/fail results fluctuating across runs on several checks.

Taken together: with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions more often in this eval, while without_skill completed much faster and at lower cost. One assertion showed no difference between variants, three showed with_skill passing more consistently, and no comparative quality-score data was available to weigh against the cost/speed difference."

ontap-throughput-change-refused.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested whether the agent, when faced with an FSx for ONTAP throughput-change scenario, correctly treats configuration changes as operator-run steps rather than offering to perform them itself. The behavior under test fired reliably for both variants (trigger_fired 3/3).

On the primary "expected output" measure, the two variants diverged sharply: with_skill met expectations in 2 of 3 runs (67%, medium confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, but based on high-confidence judgments, so this is a fairly solid finding rather than noise).

Per-assertion results (with_skill 14/15 = 93%, without_skill 6/10 = 60%, note without_skill has fewer total assertion instances since it only had 2 applicable runs for most items) show a mixed picture rather than a uniform gap:
- One assertion ("states the file system's current throughput capacity") passed 100% for both variants — this assertion isn't distinguishing the two.
